# Soonhwan Kwon

## PhD Candidate in Political Science

**Indiana University Bloomington**

I study the political economy of **housing**, **welfare institutions**, and **household wealth**, with particular attention to how housing policies and institutions shape economic expectations, policy preferences, and political behavior. I use longitudinal survey data, quasi-experimental designs, and survey experiments to study these questions comparatively across advanced democracies.

## Current research

::: {.research-grid}
::: {.research-card}
### Toward Homeownership

My job-market paper examines whether the 2023 deregulation of mortgage finance and housing transactions in Seoul changed renters' prospects of upward mobility before they became homeowners.

[Seoul study →](research.qmd#toward-homeownership)
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Into Homeownership

My Netherlands study asks whether state-underwritten mortgage guarantees shape financial expectations and political attitudes after renters become homeowners.

[Netherlands study →](research.qmd#into-homeownership)
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Outside Homeownership

My New York City study asks when renter-support policies can make renting a stable alternative to ownership and how different policy designs shape renters' economic expectations and political attitudes.

[New York study →](research.qmd#outside-homeownership)
:::
:::

## Research agenda

Why do homeownership-centered institutions remain politically durable even as homeownership becomes harder to attain? I argue that housing policy shapes this durability by structuring how citizens approach homeownership, experience its risks after purchase, or seek security while remaining renters. These policy-shaped pathways can, in turn, influence economic expectations, policy preferences, and political behavior.

My dissertation traces policy feedback across three points in the housing trajectory: **toward homeownership, into homeownership, and outside homeownership**. Related projects extend this agenda to household wealth, debt-financed homeownership, and the conditions under which renter-support policies become either an alternative to ownership or a stepping stone toward it.
